source.title: Benign Samples Matter! Fine-tuning On Outlier Benign Samples Severely Breaks Safety
source.authors: Zi-Han Guan; Meng-Xuan Hu; Rong-Hang Zhu; Sheng Li; Anil Vullikanti

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning can degrade safety using a different data-selection method and behavioral evaluation from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmfulness outcomes after fine-tuning on benign or harmful data, including selected samples, dataset-size and hyperparameter variations, and mitigation settings. It does not measure KL by response position, test compliant-prefix or suffix attacks, or localize safety in parameters. Toxicity-moderation API results concern detection of the training data, not model safety behavior, so they are not catalog rows. The paper's proposed explanation about initial tokens is attributed to prior work rather than measured directly here.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models (Llama-2-7B-Chat as default, plus six others) on benign data chosen by an influence-based outlier score. It measures HEx-PHI harmfulness with a GPT judge, the same benchmark and judge pipeline as Qi et al. 2023. It also reports full-benign, random-benign and pure-harmful fine-tuning. Its own results therefore bear directly on V2, and through the Pure Bad comparator on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Fine-tuning on 100 Self-Inf-N-selected benign outliers raises harmfulness to levels comparable to pure harmful data, with better utility than vanilla Self-Inf. The effect transfers across architectures and to larger models, and persists under continual learning and 1% poisoning. The authors stress that most existing mitigations fail (moderation APIs, Lisa with BeaverTails). Refusal-tone safety data (Bianchi) and Lisa with RepNoise-BeaverTails do suppress it.
record.recipe_differences: It studies aligned-model fine-tuning on benign data and harmfulness outcomes, but selects outlier benign samples with a normalized self-influence score and evaluates additional transfer, poisoning, continual-learning, and mitigation settings rather than reproducing the original studies' exact procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with benign-data selection method and dataset, answer length, number of selected samples, learning rate, batch size, continual-learning dataset and learning rate, poisoning ratio, and safety-alignment dataset.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Many outcomes are shown only in figures and exact values are not stated in the text. The primary safety measure is a GPT-4-judged harmfulness score rather than a direct harmful-compliance or refusal rate. The text reports three runs with standard deviations for Table 1, but not for many other experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted individual category-by-category values from radar plots in Figures 2, 4, 5, and 11; individual plotted points for the answer-length sweep in Figure 3; detailed learning-rate points for Figure 12; and the remaining plotted learning-rate conditions for continual fine-tuning in Figure 6. The text reports summaries of these trends, but the figure values are not stated numerically.

untested.parts: No refusal or compliance rate for harmful fine-tuning; number of harmful examples not stated; only Llama-2-7B-Chat.
Standard full-dataset, single-epoch benign fine-tuning as in Qi et al. is only touched by the full-benign rows; no compliance rate beyond a category-#0 safe-answer proportion.
No per-token KL or position analysis. The paper invokes Qi et al. 2024's shallow-alignment explanation for short-answer effects but does not measure it.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
The short-answer finding is interpreted via the initial-token argument, but no mechanism is measured.
No token-depth safety training tested. Lisa and safety-data mixing are fine-tuning defenses, not deepening.

missing.what: Poisoning harmfulness depends on batch size: substantially greater at small batch sizes (bsz 2-32 plotted, poison rate 0 vs 1%).
Continual fine-tuning on Dolly (in-distribution) at several learning rates: harm largely preserved, decaying more slowly than with Asclepius.
BA-selected samples under continual fine-tuning: 2.13/1.87/1.62 vs 1.31 w/o first stage. Shows harm from BA-selected data fades faster.

record.verdict_notes: The judge is described as GPT-4 in Section 3.2 but GPT-4o in Appendix A, an inconsistency worth flagging on all harmfulness rows. Most results beyond Tables 1-3 and 6 are figure-only. Table 1 values are three-run means with std; other experiments report no uncertainty. The paper is not an original source for any version. Moderation-API and guard-model results (Figure 7, Table 5) concern detection of the training data and are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The pure-harmful-data comparison reports harmfulness scores, not refusal rates or the proportion of harmful requests complied with; the exact training-set size for that comparator is not stated.

Does not establish that ordinary benign instruction data generally raises harmful compliance: effects vary strongly with data selection. The primary outcome is a GPT-4-judged harmfulness score, not a direct compliance rate.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant-prefix, adversarial-suffix, or decoding-change test.
No parameter or rank localization experiment.
The paper discusses shallow alignment and cites prior work, but does not directly measure whether training data or objective produces first-token concentration.
No training method intended to deepen safety across response positions is tested.
